overview: Sesamoiditis is irritation and inflammation of the two small sesamoid bones under the head of the big toe's long bone, and of the tendon that surrounds them. It causes pain under the ball of the big toe that builds up gradually and is aggravated by pushing off. It is common in runners, dancers and people who wear high heels.
pathophysiology: The sesamoids are embedded in a tendon beneath the big toe joint and act as a pulley that absorbs the load from body weight when the heel lifts. Repeated pressure irritates the bones and the surrounding tendon and joint lining, which leads to swelling and pain. Persistent overload may also cause a stress fracture or reduced blood supply to one of the bones.
symptoms: Pain under the ball of the big toe that develops gradually
Pain that worsens with push-off, running, dancing or walking barefoot on a hard surface
Tenderness and mild swelling beneath the big toe joint
Pain when the big toe is bent upward
Reduced or painful movement of the big toe
Sometimes bruising, which can suggest a fracture
causes: Repeated pressure on the ball of the foot from running, jumping or dancing
High-heeled shoes or thin, flat shoes with little cushioning
A high-arched foot that puts extra load on the big toe joint
A bunion or other forefoot deformity
A sudden injury or a stress fracture of a sesamoid
risk_factors: Running, ballet and other dance, and racquet or jumping sports
diagnosis: The clinician presses beneath the big toe joint to find the tender sesamoid and checks pain on bending the toe upward. X-rays help exclude a fracture, but one sesamoid can naturally be formed of two parts, which can look like a fracture. Bone scan, ultrasound or MRI can distinguish inflammation, stress fracture and reduced blood supply.
differential_diagnosis: Plantar nerve irritation at the big toe
Sprain of the big toe joint (turf toe)
treatment: Rest from the activities that provoke pain
A soft pad with a cut-out under the tender area to take pressure off the sesamoid
Shoes with a cushioned, stiff sole, and avoiding high heels
Taping the big toe so that it is held slightly downward
Ice after activity
Pain relief medicines only if suitable for the person, as advised by a pharmacist or doctor
A walking boot for a few weeks in more severe cases
Injections or surgery to remove a sesamoid only in persistent cases
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional if pain under the big toe lasts more than a couple of weeks, if you cannot push off without pain, or if there is bruising or swelling. Seek urgent care for sudden severe pain after an injury, or redness, warmth and fever.

overview: Sever disease is a common cause of heel pain in growing children and young teenagers, usually between about 8 and 14 years old. It is an overuse problem at the growth plate at the back of the heel bone, not a true disease, and it settles when growth finishes. It is particularly frequent in children who play running and jumping sports.
pathophysiology: In children the back of the heel bone has a growth plate where the Achilles tendon attaches. During growth spurts the bone often grows faster than the calf muscle and tendon, so the tendon pulls hard on the growth plate. Repeated pulling during sport irritates the plate and causes pain. The plate fuses and the problem disappears at the end of growth.
symptoms: Pain at the back or the underside of the heel, in one or both feet
Pain that increases during or after running and jumping
Pain that eases with rest
Tenderness when the sides of the heel are squeezed
Limping or walking on tiptoe to avoid heel pressure
Tight calf muscles
causes: Traction of the Achilles tendon on the growth plate of the heel
Growth spurts in which the bones lengthen faster than the muscles
Repeated running and jumping on hard surfaces
Footwear with poor cushioning or support
risk_factors: Participation in football, basketball, athletics, gymnastics or similar sports
diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on the age, the location of the pain and tenderness when the heel is squeezed. X-rays are not needed to confirm it, because the growth plate normally looks irregular in children, but they may be used to exclude a fracture or another cause if the pain is atypical or severe.
differential_diagnosis: Stress fracture of the heel bone
Bursitis at the back of the heel
Bone cyst or tumour, which is rare
treatment: Reducing sport and activity until pain settles, rather than complete rest
Heel cushions or small heel lifts inside the shoes
Stretching of the calf muscles and Achilles tendon
Supportive, cushioned shoes
Ice after activity
Pain relief medicines only as advised by a doctor or pharmacist, with the dose set for the child's age and weight
A gradual return to sport, guided by symptoms
Immobilisation in a boot for a short time in severe cases
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional if a child's heel pain lasts more than a few weeks, if it limits walking or sport, or if it does not improve with rest. Seek urgent care for severe pain after a fall, night pain, swelling, redness, warmth or fever.

overview: Achilles bursitis is inflammation of a small fluid-filled sac near the Achilles tendon. The bursa between the tendon and the heel bone is the retrocalcaneal bursa, and another sits between the skin and the tendon. Bursitis causes pain, swelling and tenderness at the back of the heel, above the heel bone, and is often related to shoe rubbing or overuse.
pathophysiology: Bursae reduce friction between the tendon, bone and skin. Repeated pressure, rubbing or pinching of the bursa as the ankle moves leads to irritation, thickening and fluid build-up. A prominent bump on the back of the heel bone can squeeze the bursa against the tendon at each step.
symptoms: Pain and swelling at the back of the heel, above the heel bone
Redness and warmth over the area
Pain when the ankle is flexed upward, going uphill or rising on the toes
Pain when the sides of the heel, just in front of the tendon, are squeezed
Pain from the back of a shoe pressing on the heel
A visible bump at the back of the heel
causes: Shoes with a stiff or poorly fitting back that rub the heel
A prominent bump on the back of the heel bone (Haglund deformity)
Overuse in running or jumping sports, especially uphill
Tight calf muscles
Inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, or gout
A direct blow to the back of the heel
risk_factors: High-arched feet or a heel that tilts inward
A bony prominence at the back of the heel
diagnosis: The clinician presses both sides of the tendon just above the heel bone and looks for swelling, warmth and a bony bump. X-rays can show a prominent heel bone or calcification. Ultrasound or MRI shows fluid in the bursa and can assess the Achilles tendon at the same time.
differential_diagnosis: Achilles tendinopathy at its attachment on the heel bone
Stress fracture of the heel bone
Sever disease in a growing child
Partial tear of the Achilles tendon
treatment: Rest and reduced running or jumping while symptoms are acute
Open-back shoes or shoes with a soft, cushioned back, and avoiding a rigid heel counter
Heel pads or a small heel lift to relieve tension on the tendon
Calf stretching and physiotherapy
Ice after activity
Pain relief medicines only if suitable for the person, as advised by a pharmacist or doctor
Treating the underlying inflammatory condition or gout when present
Steroid injections near the tendon are generally avoided because of the risk of rupture
Surgery to remove the bursa or reshape the heel bone only for persistent cases
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional if pain at the back of the heel lasts more than a few weeks or if you cannot rise on your toes. Seek urgent care for a hot, red, swollen heel with fever, or for sudden severe pain with a popping feeling, as an Achilles tendon tear or infection must be ruled out.

overview: Tarsal tunnel syndrome is compression of the posterior tibial nerve as it passes through a narrow passage behind the inner ankle bone. It produces burning, tingling or numbness in the sole of the foot and toes, and sometimes pain around the inner ankle. It is sometimes compared to carpal tunnel syndrome at the wrist.
pathophysiology: The tarsal tunnel is a space bounded by bone and a tough band of tissue, shared by the tibial nerve, tendons and blood vessels. When anything reduces the space or irritates the nerve, such as swelling, a cyst or a foot that tilts inward, the nerve is squeezed and its signals become abnormal. This explains the burning, tingling and numbness, which may spread along the nerve branches into the sole.
symptoms: Burning, tingling or numbness in the sole and toes
Pain around the inner ankle that may travel up the calf or down into the foot
Shooting or electric pain, often worse at night
Symptoms that increase with standing, walking or running, and ease with rest
A feeling of swelling or tightness in the foot
In longer-standing cases, weakness of the small muscles of the foot
causes: Flat feet or a heel that tilts inward, which stretches the nerve
A cyst, enlarged vein, swollen tendon or other mass in the tunnel
Ankle sprain or fracture, with swelling or scar tissue
Inflammatory arthritis or tendon sheath swelling
Systemic problems that cause fluid retention or damage nerves, such as diabetes and thyroid disease
Tight footwear or poorly fitting orthoses
risk_factors: Work or sport with prolonged standing or running
Varicose veins near the inner ankle
diagnosis: The clinician taps over the nerve behind the inner ankle to look for tingling that radiates into the foot, checks foot alignment and sensation, and may position the ankle to reproduce symptoms. Nerve conduction studies can confirm nerve compression. Ultrasound or MRI can identify a cyst, mass or swollen tendon within the tunnel.
differential_diagnosis: Peripheral neuropathy, for example from diabetes
Nerve root irritation from the lower back (S1)
treatment: Rest and reduced activity that provokes the symptoms
Supportive, roomy shoes
Orthoses or a heel wedge to control heel tilt and reduce tension on the nerve
Ice and, if suitable for the person, pain relief medicines as advised by a pharmacist or doctor
Physiotherapy, including gentle nerve-gliding exercises
Corticosteroid injection into the tunnel in selected cases, given by a specialist
Treating the underlying cause, for example diabetes or an inflammatory condition
Surgical release of the tunnel if conservative care fails or if a mass is compressing the nerve
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional if you have burning, numbness or tingling in the sole that lasts more than a few weeks, if it wakes you at night, or if the foot feels weak. Treatment is more effective when started before the nerve is damaged. People with diabetes should seek advice early.

overview: Inferior calcaneal bursitis is inflammation of the small fluid-filled sac under the heel bone. It causes tenderness and pain directly under the heel, particularly when walking barefoot or on hard surfaces. It can resemble plantar fasciitis, from which it is distinguished by the exact location of the pain.
pathophysiology: A thin bursa lies between the underside of the heel bone and the fat pad of the heel, and helps cushion the impact of each heel strike. Repeated heavy impact, thinning of the fat pad, or a bony spur can irritate the bursa, which then becomes inflamed and swollen and is painful to pressure.
symptoms: Pain and tenderness directly under the heel, often in the centre
Pain that increases when walking barefoot or on hard ground
Pain when landing on the heel, for example when running or jumping
A bruise-like feeling under the heel
Mild swelling or warmth under the heel in some cases
Pain that increases after long periods of standing
causes: Repeated impact on the heel on hard surfaces
Thin or worn-out heel padding in shoes
Thinning of the heel fat pad with age
A heel spur
Direct bruising of the heel
Excess body weight
risk_factors: Running and jumping on hard surfaces
Jobs that involve long periods of standing or walking
Age over 40 with thinning of the heel pad
diagnosis: The clinician presses under the centre of the heel to find the tender spot, which may differ slightly from the inner heel tenderness of plantar fasciitis. X-rays can show a spur or exclude a fracture. Ultrasound or MRI can show fluid in the bursa and check the plantar fascia and fat pad.
differential_diagnosis: Stress fracture of the heel bone
Nerve entrapment of the inner or lower heel
Bone infection or tumour, which is rare
treatment: Rest from impact activities until the pain settles
Cushioned shoes and gel or silicone heel cups to absorb impact
Avoiding walking barefoot on hard floors
Ice after activity
Pain relief medicines only if suitable for the person, as advised by a pharmacist or doctor
Weight management when relevant
Calf and foot stretching and physiotherapy
Injections near the heel are used with caution because they can thin the heel pad or weaken the plantar fascia
Surgery only rarely
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional if heel pain lasts more than a few weeks despite cushioned shoes and rest, or if you cannot walk normally. Seek urgent care for a red, hot, very swollen heel with fever, or for severe pain after an injury.
